column1: # THE KIND GATE MUST SURVIVE A CLONE.
# A preference is a default, so a concrete peer replaces it -- but only
# where the peer is the same KIND of thing (`*1 & 2` is 2; `*1 & {}` is an
# error). The gate is the preferred value's own `superpeg`. It once widened
# to the numeric FAMILY, which also let `*8080 & 3.5` through; see
# test/spec/number-tower.tsv for the rows that pin the narrower rule.
# Uncloned, both ports already refused: `x:*1&{}` errors in both. Every row
# below reaches the PrefVal through a clone -- a spread template, a $ref, a
# copy() -- which is where Go dropped the gate entirely and accepted a map,
# a string, a boolean or a list as an override. Not weakened: absent.
# The last two rows are the ones that must NOT move. A gate that rejects
# everything would pass all the error rows above and break the language.
# THE GATE IS A SCALAR GATE. The rows above all have a SCALAR preferred
# value, whose superior() is its kind -- so the gate has something to
# refuse with. A structural preferred value does not: a map and a list
# inherit FeatureVal.superior(), which is TOP, and `unite(top, peer)` is
# the peer, so ANY peer overrides a structural default including one of
# another kind entirely. That is why `*1 & "s"` is a conflict and
# Recorded here rather than fixed: it long predates the kind gate (it is
# what FeatureVal's superior has always meant), both ports agree on it,
# and giving maps and lists a real kind yardstick is its own change with
# its own decisions -- what `*{x:1} & {y:2}` should then mean, not least,
# since today the default is REPLACED rather than merged. These rows
# exist so that change cannot be made by accident, in one port only, or
# without noticing which of the two behaviours moved.
# The scalar direction of the same pairing, for contrast: a scalar
# default DOES refuse a map, which is the gate doing its work.
# A preference inside a COLON-CHAIN nested map (issue #1). The report was
# that `bar: kind: *'led' | 'custom'` raised a model error naming both
# alternatives; it resolves to the preferred one in both engines. The
# canon row is the one that matters -- gen alone cannot see that the
# alternatives are still there, unresolved, behind the preference.
# ... and the preference yields when the other alternative is required.
